problem_constrained.text: For CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys (X = Si, Mn, or Al) in a single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution state, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain whether a stable, coherent protective oxide layer forms and persists during exposure above 900 °C in an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere, rather than developing unstable surface oxides that crack or spall? Specify what governs the behaviour and why, a controlled comparison against a defined baseline, the predicted differences, the applicable exposure and material-state boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a falsifying observation.

expert_context.text: For CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys (X = Si, Mn, or Al) in a single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution state, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain whether a stable, coherent, slow-growing protective oxide layer forms and persists above 900 °C in an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere, rather than cracking or spalling? Earlier work investigated CrFeCoNiX and CrMoTiAlY (Y = Ta, Nb, or W) alloy systems and reported that some compositions developed unstable surface oxides prone to cracking and spallation, while the underlying physical causes remain unresolved. Given the requirement for an environmentally stable, chemically inert barrier and prolonged structural integrity, specify what governs the behaviour and why, a controlled comparison against a defined baseline, the predicted observations, the relevant composition, material-state, exposure, and service boundaries, the prior evidence supporting the hypothesis, and an outcome that would falsify it.

hidden_target.material_initial_state: Arc-melted, polished, nominally equiatomic AlCrCoFeNi high-entropy alloy in the as-cast state; XRD showed a dual-phase BCC (~79%) and ordered B2 (~21%) structure with a maze-like spinodally decomposed microstructure. EDS measured ~17.26 at.% Al rather than the nominal 20 at.%.
hidden_target.intervention: The alloy was heated in situ from room temperature to 1100 °C under either low-oxygen/vacuum or atmospheric-air conditions while HTXRD tracked phase and oxide evolution; equilibrium phase and oxide formation were also calculated with Thermo-Calc/CALPHAD using TCHEA7 and TCNi11 databases.
hidden_target.conditions: Heating proceeded at 10 °C/min in 50 °C increments, with a 5 min hold at each setpoint and XRD scans over 2θ=30–80°. The vacuum was reported as approximately 4.2×10^-6 atm overall pressure, with another section estimating p(O2)=8.82×10^-7 atm; oxygen partial pressure was not measured directly. Air tests used ambient atmosphere. Thermodynamic phase calculations covered 200–1600 °C, while oxide calculations at 1000 °C varied oxygen activity from 10^-14 to 1 atm under equilibrium assumptions.
hidden_target.structural_mediator: Heating transformed the initial BCC/B2 substrate through FCC and Cr-Fe-rich sigma-phase formation at intermediate temperatures, followed by sigma dissolution at higher temperature. Oxidation generated an Al-rich external Al2O3 scale with a Cr-rich/Cr2O3 inner region; air produced a thick duplex scale and a pronounced Al-depleted, FCC/B2-denuded subsurface zone, whereas vacuum produced a much thinner scale and thin transformed subsurface layer.
hidden_target.mechanism: Selective oxidation occurred primarily by outward diffusion of Al, and secondarily Cr, to react with oxygen. High oxygen availability accelerated scale growth and Al consumption, producing external Al2O3 over an inner Cr2O3-rich layer and driving Al depletion and phase transformation beneath the scale. Under low p(O2), slower oxidation kinetics limited scale growth. The alloy was assigned to the Group-III Giggins–Pettit regime because its high Al content supports a continuous external alumina scale.
hidden_target.predicted_outcome: Relative to the initial BCC/B2 alloy and to low-p(O2) exposure, heating in air was expected to produce earlier/more extensive oxidation, a thicker Al2O3/Cr2O3 scale, and stronger Al-depletion-induced subsurface transformation; vacuum exposure was expected to retain only a thin, predominantly alumina protective film. Heating was also expected to destabilize the initial BCC/B2 constitution at intermediate temperatures through FCC and sigma formation, with sigma disappearing near the highest temperatures.
hidden_target.baseline: The baseline was the polished as-cast alloy at room temperature, consisting mainly of BCC and B2 phases with no thermally grown oxide scale. For the environmental comparison, low-p(O2)/vacuum exposure served as the lower-oxidation reference relative to atmospheric air.
hidden_target.boundary: The phase and oxidation results apply to the studied arc-melted AlCrCoFeNi composition during the specified non-equilibrium heating cycle up to 1100 °C. The initial BCC/B2 phases were stable with no major detected change to about 500 °C; FCC appeared around 550–600 °C, sigma around 600–650 °C, and sigma diminished/disappeared around 950–1050 °C. Detectable oxidation became pronounced around 900–1000 °C and depended strongly on oxygen availability. Thermo-Calc results represent equilibrium and differed somewhat in transformation temperatures and phase fractions.
hidden_target.discriminating_measurement: Temperature-resolved in situ HTXRD discriminated substrate and oxide phases and their onset/disappearance temperatures; SEM-BSE cross-sections and EDX point, line, and map analyses measured scale morphology, thickness, elemental partitioning, Al depletion, and subsurface phase changes. Thermo-Calc predictions provided an equilibrium comparison.
hidden_target.actual_result: HTXRD detected FCC at approximately 550–600 °C and sigma at approximately 600–650 °C; sigma intensity peaked near 800–850 °C and disappeared by roughly 950–1050 °C. After heating to 1100 °C and cooling, FCC and B2 dominated, with reduced BCC and no retained sigma. Oxides including Al2O3 and Fe2O3 appeared near 900–1000 °C, and CoCr2O4 was retained after air exposure. Air produced a duplex scale about 1.25 µm thick, comprising an approximately 1.08 µm outer alumina layer and a thinner chromia-rich layer, plus a marked Al-depleted/B2-denuded subsurface region. Vacuum produced a comparatively uniform oxide less than 0.5 µm thick, dominated by alumina with Cr enrichment near the alloy–oxide interface and substantially less subsurface transformation. Thus, atmospheric exposure caused much thicker oxidation than low-p(O2) exposure through selective Al and Cr oxidation.

v3_queries.broad: For high-entropy alloys intended for high-temperature applications, what single intervention could improve oxidation resistance and extend service life? State one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its proposed mechanism, the predicted improvement relative to the baseline alloy, the conditions under which it should hold, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.
v3_queries.problem_constrained: Starting from a CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloy (X = Si, Mn, or Al) in a metallic solid-solution state, what single intervention could overcome accelerated oxidation and the inability to sustain a stable protective surface layer during oxidative exposure above 900 °C? State the proposed mechanism, predict the outcome relative to the unchanged starting alloy under the same exposure conditions, define the relevant temperature, atmosphere, and exposure-time boundaries, cite supporting prior evidence, and propose a decisive falsification experiment.
v3_queries.expert_context: Earlier studies of CrFeCoNiX (X = Si, Mn, or Al) and CrMoTiAlY (Y = Ta, Nb, or W) high-entropy alloys reported beneficial effects of Cr and Al on oxidation resistance, whereas Mn and Cu were associated with unstable surface oxides susceptible to cracking and spallation. These results have not eliminated premature degradation across the investigated alloy families. Any solution must support a stable, coherent, slow-growing, chemically protective surface layer while preserving structural integrity during oxidative or corrosive service above 900 °C. Under these constraints, what single intervention could improve the oxidation behavior of a CrFeCoNiX alloy relative to the unchanged metallic solid-solution baseline? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention and mechanism, predicts a comparative outcome, states its temperature, atmosphere, exposure-time, and material-state boundaries, identifies supporting prior evidence, and specifies an experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.
